title: What If We Sent a Dog Into Orbit? We Did in 1957, and Hid the Truth for 45 Years

scenes.text: What if the first creature in orbit was a stray dog? The official story was a lie.
November 3, 1957. Four weeks after Sputnik, the Soviet Union launches Sputnik 2, with a six-kilo Moscow street dog named Laika strapped inside.
Her pulse triples during launch. There was never a plan to bring her home, and the cooling system was rushed to make a political deadline.
Moscow said she lived for about a week in orbit, then was painlessly put to sleep. Textbooks repeated it for decades.
In 2002 a Russian scientist revealed the truth: the cabin overheated, and Laika died within five to seven hours of liftoff.
The capsule kept circling, 2,570 orbits, until it burned up in April 1958. Her flight lasted hours. Her coffin flew for five months.

description:
What if we sent a dog into orbit? On 3 November 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2 with Laika, a roughly 6 kg stray from the streets of Moscow, making her the first living creature to orbit Earth. There was never a plan to return her.
Soviet accounts said she survived six or seven days and was then euthanised. In 2002 Dimitri Malashenkov of Moscow's Institute of Biomedical Problems revealed that her pulse tripled at launch and that she died of overheating and stress only five to seven hours into the flight, after life-support systems were rushed to meet the anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution. Sputnik 2 completed about 2,570 orbits before burning up on 14 April 1958.
